claims.claim: Greenwood writes by imagining he is present, smelling and tasting what characters do, then writing down enough for the reader to see the crypt or court.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: I'm smelling what the characters are smelling

claims.claim: Greenwood writes what publishers ask for, in the way they want it, and still entertainingly.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: I write about what publishers ask me to

claims.claim: Greenwood's advice: never think your words are perfect; rewrite anything weak or awkward.
claims.quote: Never think your words are perfect

claims.claim: Crawford reads a rule first as written, in context and without regard to intent, because the published text must stand on its own.
claims.source: Sage Advice Compendium (Jeremy Crawford, Wizards of the Coast, v2.7 2021)
claims.quote: The text is forced to stand on its own.

claims.feature: rules as foundation, DM as bridge
claims.claim: 5e's rules deliberately lay a foundation for the DM to build on rather than trying to cover every contingency.
claims.source: Sage Advice Compendium (Jeremy Crawford, Wizards of the Coast, v2.7 2021)
claims.quote: no set of rules could reasonably account for every contingency

claims.claim: Only the compendium is official; designers' tweets and public statements are advice.
claims.source: Sage Advice Compendium (Jeremy Crawford, Wizards of the Coast, v2.7 2021)
claims.quote: are not official rulings; they are advice

claims.claim: The 2024 PHB teaches key terms (D20 Test, Magic action) in an opening play guide with examples of play and sidebars, and summarizes rules terminology in a glossary appendix.
claims.source: What's New in the 2024 Player's Handbook? (Michael Galvis, D&D Beyond, 2024-09-17)
claims.quote: key terms of the game, like what a D20 Test

claims.claim: The 2024 PHB renames terms via an Updated Terminology Table: Race to Species, Cast a Spell action to Magic action, Ki to Monk's Focus.
claims.source: Updates in the Player's Handbook (2024) (D&D Beyond staff, 2024-09-03)
claims.quote: uses some new terms, as shown in the Updated Terminology Table

claims.feature: headers and bullets for the DM's eye
claims.claim: Merwin: use headers, subheaders and bullets to draw the DM's eye to the right information at the right time.
claims.source: Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer (Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2020-03-25)
claims.quote: Use headers and subheaders to call out breaks in information

claims.claim: Goodman Games designer Burnside (2025) says boxed text must be short, evocative and helpful, and that his 2018 boxes carried too many distractions.
claims.source: Read aloud text in modules: What are folks opinions, page 10 (EN World, 2025)
claims.quote: short, evocative, and helpful to the DM and players
claims.page: forum (posts by a Goodman Games designer)

claims.claim: Crawford: the 2025 core books are filled with lore nuggets because WotC will not assume readers own the old books.
claims.source: D&D's Jeremy Crawford on the 2025 Monster Manual, The New Starter Set, and High Level Gameplay (CBR, 2025-02-05)

claims.claim: Mearls (2025) credits a collaborator with making sure a third-party manuscript matched the D&D house style, confirming an internal style exists even where none is published.
claims.quote: everything matched the D&D house style

claims.claim: The 2019 guide (v1.08a) rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th edition, and covers only D&D-specific departures from them.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: The general rules bind every D&D product, not just rulebooks.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: whether RPG books, board games, novels, or something else

claims.claim: Editions are spelled out and lowercased ('fifth edition'), with 4E/5E abbreviations confined to tables, conversion documents, or informal text.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We write “fifth edition,” for instance, not “5th Edition.”
